hints: Focus on whether melting breaks the strong bonds inside a molecule or just the weaker forces between separate molecules.
Spot which substance is a giant covalent lattice with no separate molecules, where every atom is joined by covalent bonds.
Ask yourself which structures still exist as intact molecules after melting, so only intermolecular forces were overcome.
walkthrough:
**Sort by structure type**

Think like a teacher sorting particles. Is it giant covalent, simple molecular, or hydrogen-bonded molecular?

Structures: $\text{SiO}_2$ is giant covalent, $\text{I}_2$ is simple molecular, $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ (ice) and ethanol are molecular with hydrogen bonding.

**Remember what melting does**

Melting gives particles enough energy to move past each other. It normally overcomes only the forces *between* molecules.

Rule: intermolecular forces broken on melting, covalent bonds inside molecules stay intact.

**Apply to giant vs molecular**

In $\text{SiO}_2$, there are no separate molecules. The whole lattice is one network of $\text{Si-O}$ covalent bonds.

$$\text{giant lattice (solid)} \rightarrow \text{mobile atoms (liquid): Si-O covalent bonds must break}$$

**Check the others stay as molecules**

Ice melts to water, iodine melts to liquid $\text{I}_2$, ethanol melts to liquid ethanol. The $\text{O-H}$, $\text{I-I}$ and $\text{C-C}$ covalent bonds are still there.

Conclusion: only the giant covalent substance must break covalent bonds to melt.

options.A: Silicon(IV) oxide, $\text{SiO}_2$, is a giant covalent macromolecule. Every Si is covalently bonded to four O atoms in a continuous lattice. To melt it, these strong $\text{Si-O}$ covalent bonds must be broken, which is why it has a very high melting point.
options.B: Ice is wrong. Solid $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ is held together by hydrogen bonds between molecules. On melting, hydrogen bonds are partially broken but the covalent $\text{O-H}$ bonds inside each water molecule remain intact.
options.C: Iodine is wrong. It exists as discrete $\text{I}_2$ molecules held together by London dispersion forces. Melting overcomes these weak intermolecular forces, while the strong $\text{I-I}$ covalent bond inside each molecule is unchanged.
options.D: Ethanol is wrong. Liquid and solid ethanol contain intact $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ molecules. Melting breaks hydrogen bonds and van der Waals forces between molecules, not the covalent $\text{C-C}$, $\text{C-H}$, $\text{C-O}$ or $\text{O-H}$ bonds.
